title: PrimorialInterval: The Natural Sieve Domain
content: The primorial interval I(l) = (l!, (l+1)!] is the fundamental organizing structure for the Selberg sieve approach. For any prime p in I(l), the factorials 0!, 1!, ..., l! are exactly those less than p. So AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite(p) requires precisely l+1 conditions: each p - k! for k = 0, ..., l must be composite.
significance: The primorial interval decomposition converts the infinite quantifier 'all k with k! < p' into a finite count 'all k ≤ l' where l is the interval level. This finitization is what makes the Selberg sieve applicable at each level independently.

title: Interval Size l · l!: The Sieve Denominator
content: |I(l)| = l · l! elements. Proved using Nat.card_Ioc (cardinality of half-open intervals) together with factorial recursion (l+1)! = (l+1)·l! so (l+1)! - l! = l·l!. The size grows super-exponentially, which ensures the sieve works: the 'bad' prime count (O((l+1)·l!/(log l!)²)) is smaller than the total prime count (≈ l!/log(l!)).
mathContext: $|I(l)| = (l+1)! - l! = l \cdot l!$. Growth: $|I(1)| = 1$, $|I(2)| = 4$, $|I(3)| = 18$, $|I(4)| = 96$, $|I(5)| = 600$. By PNT, $\#\{\text{primes in } I(l)\} \approx l!/\log(l!)$, which grows faster than the bad count $\ll (l+1) \cdot l!/(\log(l!))^2$.
significance: The size formula is needed both for the qualitative sieve argument (more primes than bad primes) and as a technical ingredient in other proofs. The key growth rate comparison is l!/log(l!) vs. (l+1)·l!/(log l!)², with ratio log(l!)/(l+1) → ∞.

title: factorial_bound_in_interval: The Level Bound Lemma
content: If p lies in I(l) and k! < p, then k ≤ l. This bounds the universal quantifier in AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite(p) to the finite set {0,...,l}. Proof by contradiction: if k > l, then (l+1)! ≤ k! but also (l+1)! ≥ p, giving k! ≥ p, contradicting k! < p.
mathContext: Proof: $p \in I(l)$ gives $p \leq (l+1)!$. If $k > l$ then $k \geq l+1$, so $k! \geq (l+1)!$ by factorial monotonicity, giving $k! \geq p$, contradicting $k! < p$. This makes AFSC(p) for $p \in I(l)$ a finite condition: check only $k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, l\}$.
significance: Without this bound, AFSC would be an infinite condition (for all k with k! < p). The level structure converts it to a finite check at each level, which is essential for the sieve to count bad primes at each level l independently.

title: BadFactorialIndices: The Sieve Target Set
content: For candidate prime p at level l, the bad factorial indices are those k ≤ l where p - k! is prime. AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite holds iff this set is empty (with the ≥ 2 side condition). The Selberg sieve bounds the number of p ∈ I(l) with nonempty bad set — and condition_count_at_level confirms |Bad(p,l)| ≤ l+1 (trivially, since it's a subset of {0,...,l}).
mathContext: $\mathrm{Bad}(p, l) = \{k \leq l : p - k! \in \mathbb{P}\} \subseteq \{0, 1, \ldots, l\}$. So $|\mathrm{Bad}(p,l)| \leq l+1$. Each bad index $k$ witnesses $p \in \{n \in I(l) : n - k! \in \mathbb{P}\}$ — a shifted prime set of size $\ll l!/(\log l!)^2$ by Brun-Titchmarsh.
significance: The BadFactorialIndices structure makes explicit what the sieve is counting. The union bound over k = 0,...,l gives the key inequality: bad prime count ≤ (l+1) × Brun-Titchmarsh bound = O((l+1)·l!/(log l!)²), which is smaller than the total prime count for large l.

title: selberg_density_axiom: The Analytic Boundary
content: selberg_density_axiom asserts that for l ≥ 3, some prime p ∈ I(l) satisfies AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite. This is the single axiom separating the fully proved structural machinery from the analytic number theory that completes the argument. The axiom is an existence statement, not a density estimate — the actual Selberg argument gives a count ≫ l!/(log l!)², making existence obvious for l ≥ 3.
mathContext: The Selberg $\lambda^2$ upper bound sieve gives: $\#\{n \in I(l) : n - k! \in \mathbb{P}\} \leq \frac{2l!}{\log(l!) \cdot \log(l!/\log l!)}$. Union over $k = 0, \ldots, l$: bad prime count $\ll (l+1) \cdot l!/(\log l!)^2$. Since total primes in $I(l) \approx l!/\log(l!)$ by PNT, the good fraction $\to 1$. For $l \geq 3$, the good count is positive.
significance: This axiom crystallizes exactly where formalization currently stops. The structural work (primorial intervals, sieve objects, disjointness, conditional implication) is fully proved. What remains is formalizing the analytic toolchain: PNT for intervals, Brun-Titchmarsh inequality, and the Selberg λ² sieve. These represent deep open challenges in Lean/Mathlib.

title: selberg_implies_erdos: Infinitude from Per-Level Density
content: The main conditional theorem: the density axiom implies Erdős #1059. For any N, take l = N + 3 ≥ 3 and use the axiom to get p ∈ I(l) qualifying. Since p > l! ≥ N + 3 > N, we have p > N. The primorial_intervals_disjoint lemma ensures primes from different levels are distinct, so the map l ↦ p_l injects into the qualifying prime set — proving it's infinite.
mathContext: Proof uses Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt: for $\{n : \mathbb{N} \mid P(n)\}$ to be infinite, it suffices to show $\forall N, \exists p > N$ with $P(p)$. Take $l = N+3$: by selberg_density_axiom, $\exists p \in I(l)$ qualifying. Then $p > l! \geq N+3 > N$ by Nat.self_le_factorial.
significance: The proof structure cleanly separates the analytic content (the axiom) from the combinatorial content (the infinitude argument). This is a model for conditional formalization: fully prove the deduction chain, axiomatize only the genuinely hard analytic claim, and make the assumption explicit.
